meta.description: John Lennon never said it. Mark Lewisohn and Snopes trace the gag to a 1981 BBC Radio 4 Radio Active sketch written by Geoffrey Perkins.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Ringo isn't even the best drummer in the Beatles'?
meta.ogDescription: Lennon never said it. The earliest known source is a 1981 Radio Active sketch by Geoffrey Perkins, per Mark Lewisohn and Snopes.

answer.label: Not John Lennon — actually Geoffrey Perkins
answer.sourceLine: Beatles historian Mark Lewisohn — who has read and heard every surviving Lennon interview — says Lennon never said this, and Snopes rates the attribution “Incorrect Attribution” ↗. The earliest known source is a sketch written by Geoffrey Perkins for BBC Radio 4’s spoof-local-radio comedy Radio Active, broadcast in 1981 — the year after Lennon was murdered.
answer.confidenceText: No Lennon interview, recording or transcript contains it; the traceable origin is a 1981 radio comedy script.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from
source.excerpt: Alright, maybe Ringo Starr wasn’t the best drummer in the world. Alright, maybe he wasn’t the best drummer in the Beatles, but he’s a name.
trail: Wikiquote places the line in its Misattributed section ↗, calling it an apocryphal, jokey attribution to Lennon — and points readers at the Snopes fact-check.

In a 2013 interview, Mark Lewisohn said he had heard and read every Lennon interview and never found it: “John Lennon never said it — and wouldn’t have said it.” ↗ At that stage he still believed it began as a comedian’s 1983 television gag.

In 2018 the trail went back further. Radio X recounts how Tim Worthington found the joke in a 1981 edition of Radio Active ↗, after which Lewisohn located the episode and confirmed from BBC paperwork that the script was Geoffrey Perkins’s.
Snopes reproduces Lewisohn’s finding and rates the Lennon attribution “Incorrect Attribution” ↗, while cautioning that further scholarship may yet uncover earlier antecedents.
source.excerptNote: The sketch line as transcribed in Wikipedia’s article on Radio Active ↗. The version that circulates online — “Ringo isn’t even the best drummer in the Beatles” — is a compressed folk retelling of it, not a verbatim quotation of anyone.

sourceLink.text: Snopes: Did John Lennon say it? (Incorrect Attribution)

source.rightsNote: The exact one-liner that circulates has no identifiable author — it is an anonymous compression of a sketch, so no public-domain claim can honestly be made for it. The underlying 1981 Radio Active script is a modern BBC broadcast work written by Geoffrey Perkins and would not be public domain; quotle.info quotes only the short transcribed line for fact-checking purposes.

author.name: Geoffrey Perkins
author.heading: The man who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: 1953–2008 · British comedy writer & producer · Radio Active, Father Ted, Have I Got News for You
author.bio: Geoffrey Howard Perkins was one of the most quietly influential figures in British comedy: he produced the original radio series of The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, co-created and performed in the Radio 4 spoof-station series Radio Active, and later helped bring Spitting Image, Have I Got News for You and Father Ted to air. From 1995 to 2001 he was BBC Television’s Head of Comedy, a stretch that produced The Royle Family, The Fast Show and Coupling. He died suddenly in 2008 — and one of his throwaway 1981 radio gags has outlived the credit, travelling the world for decades under John Lennon’s name.

misattribution.heading: How a radio gag became a Lennon quote
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-repeated “Lennon” lines in music writing, and it has been printed as fact by national newspapers. It has never been found in a single interview, recording or transcript.

items.why: Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗, describing it as apocryphally and jokingly attributed to Lennon in an interview where he was supposedly asked whether Ringo was the best drummer in the world. Lewisohn’s point is blunt: if Lennon “famously” said it, there should be a record of when.
For years the gag was credited to a 1983 television appearance by the British comedian — a claim Snopes reports came from Carrott’s own office ↗. The 1981 Radio Active recording predates it.
Lewisohn singled the paper out for stating that Lennon had “famously” said it: “John Lennon never said that, famously or otherwise” ↗.
The circulating one-liner is not a verbatim transcript of anything. The sketch line as transcribed ↗ is longer, and ends with the real punchline — “but he’s a name.”

misattribution.truthLine: The joke is Geoffrey Perkins’s, written for BBC Radio 4’s Radio Active in 1981 — the year after Lennon was killed. Snopes: Incorrect Attribution ↗.

context.heading: Why the line stuck to Lennon
lead: The joke only works if you believe two things: that Ringo Starr was a mediocre drummer, and that Paul McCartney — who took the kit on Back in the U.S.S.R. and The Ballad of John and Yoko — was better. Lennon believed neither. In a Playboy interview conducted in 1980, months before he was murdered, he was asked point-blank about Ringo’s musicianship and answered that Ringo was underrated, and stood up with any rock musician ↗.

What makes this misattribution unusually well-documented is that someone went looking. Pop-culture writer Tim Worthington was working through old episodes of Radio Active, Radio 4’s parody of terrible local radio, when the gag turned up in a 1981 edition; Lewisohn then pulled the episode and the BBC paperwork, which credited the script to Geoffrey Perkins ↗. A line that had spent decades as Lennon’s sharpest one-liner turned out to belong to a comedy writer who was never asked.
context.detailsSummary: The wording drifts — and that is the tell
detailsBody: No two versions of this “quote” agree. It circulates as “He’s not even the best drummer in the Beatles,” as “Ringo wasn’t even the best drummer in the Beatles,” and as a set-up-and-punchline exchange in which an interviewer supposedly asks whether Ringo is the best drummer in the world. Genuine quotations tend to stabilise around a printed text; folk jokes keep reshaping themselves to fit the teller.

Sources also still disagree on the fine detail of the 1981 broadcast. Radio X reports Lewisohn dating the episode to 6 October 1981 with the line voiced by Philip Pope, while Wikipedia’s articles on Perkins, Pope and Michael Fenton Stevens give 15 September 1981 and note that Fenton Stevens later said he was the one who delivered it. What every account agrees on is the programme, the year, and the writer.
context.pull: Ringo is a damn good drummer.
